units.name: application-core
units.role: The FastAPI application class that developers instantiate and configure, and the package's public export list.
units.description: This is the object a developer creates once per project to build their web service. It ties together routing, request validation, security, error handling and auto-generated documentation into one thing a web server can talk to, and it is the object developers configure with a title, middleware, and startup/shutdown behavior. The package's front door (its __init__.py) decides exactly which names, like FastAPI itself or the Depends helper, become visible to someone who writes 'from fastapi import ...'. This unit must never itself perform real networking, file access, or business logic — it only assembles and delegates to the specialized pieces that do the actual work.

units.name: routing
units.role: Turns decorated Python functions into HTTP path operations and WebSocket routes, matches incoming requests, runs the request-handling pipeline, and can serve a static frontend build.
units.description: This is the machinery that takes the functions a developer writes and decorates, like a function that handles GET /items/{id}, and turns them into real, working web endpoints. When a request comes in, it figures out which endpoint should handle it, checks the request's data against what the endpoint expects, calls the endpoint after running anything it depends on first, and converts the return value into a proper response. It also lets routers be nested inside other routers, and can serve a folder of pre-built frontend files (like a React app's build output) as a fallback when no API route matches, so one app can serve both an API and a web UI.

units.name: param-declarations
units.role: The marker classes and public functions (Path, Query, Header, Cookie, Body, Form, File, Depends, Security) developers use in endpoint signatures to declare where each parameter comes from and how it is validated.
units.description: This unit is the vocabulary FastAPI gives developers to describe incoming request data. When someone writes a web endpoint and wants to say a value comes from the URL path, the query string, a header, a cookie, the JSON body, submitted form data, an uploaded file, or another function that must run first, they call functions like Path(), Query(), Header(), Body(), Form(), File(), Depends() or Security(). Behind each function is a matching internal class that stores the same information in a form the rest of FastAPI can inspect later, when it is time to validate a request or generate documentation.

units.name: dependency-injection
units.role: Builds a tree of a route's parameters and sub-dependencies, resolves and calls them in order for each request, and cleans up dependencies that behave like context managers.
units.description: When a web endpoint asks for things like 'the current logged-in user' or 'a database session' by listing them as function parameters with special defaults, this unit is the machinery that figures out ahead of time what the endpoint and everything it depends on actually needs, then for every request runs those dependency functions in the right order, reuses results needed more than once in the same request, hands each function the arguments it asked for, and once the request is finished, closes any dependency that opened a resource it needs to release, such as a database connection.

A developer declares a BackgroundTasks parameter in their route function, then calls add_task with the function they want run later; FastAPI takes care of running it once the response has gone out.

units.name: openapi-generation
units.role: Builds the OpenAPI schema document describing an app's routes and models, and renders the interactive documentation pages (Swagger UI, ReDoc) that reference it.
units.description: This unit is responsible for describing an API in a standard machine-readable format and for showing that description to humans as interactive documentation. It walks through every route, parameter, and data model an application defines and turns them into the OpenAPI schema that tools like Swagger UI and ReDoc understand, and it generates the actual HTML pages (the /docs and /redoc pages seen in a browser) that load those UIs and point them at the generated schema, plus a small helper page used to complete OAuth2 login redirects inside Swagger UI.

units.name: security-schemes
units.role: Declarative security-scheme classes (API key, HTTP Basic/Bearer/Digest, OAuth2 flows, OpenID Connect) used as FastAPI dependencies to extract and validate credentials from a request and describe themselves for OpenAPI.
units.description: This part of FastAPI gives developers ready-made building blocks for adding login and authentication checks to their application. Instead of writing custom code to pull an API key out of a URL, a password out of a login form, or a bearer token out of a header, a developer attaches one of these pre-built security-scheme objects to the part of their app that needs protecting. Each scheme knows how to look for its kind of credential in an incoming request, reject the request with a clear error if it's missing, and describe itself so the automatically generated documentation shows users how to authenticate. These schemes never fetch anything over the network themselves; the OpenID Connect scheme only records a URL for documentation purposes.

units.name: pydantic-compat
units.role: Isolates the rest of FastAPI from Pydantic's internal APIs behind one interface for field metadata, model construction, JSON-schema generation, and validation/serialization.
units.description: FastAPI is built on top of a separate library called Pydantic, which checks that data is the right shape and converts it to and from JSON. Pydantic's own internal building blocks can change between versions, so this unit acts as a translator layer: the rest of FastAPI asks it simple questions like 'is this field required?' or 'turn this model into a JSON schema', and this unit does the work of talking to Pydantic directly. That way, if Pydantic changes internally, only this one area needs updating instead of the whole codebase.

units.description: This unit is the translator that turns whatever data a developer returns from their endpoint, such as dates, custom classes, or database results, into the simple text-and-number format that can be sent over the internet as JSON. Without it, FastAPI would not know how to convert rich Python data into the format web clients expect.

units.name: errors
units.role: Defines the exception types FastAPI and user code raise for HTTP, WebSocket, and validation errors, and the default handlers that turn those exceptions into responses.
units.description: This unit is FastAPI's error vocabulary. It defines the different kinds of problems that can happen while handling a request or a WebSocket connection, such as a client sending bad data or a request that fails validation, as distinct named exception types. It also provides the default logic for turning those errors into something a client can receive: an HTTP error response with a status code and message, a JSON list of validation problems, or a closed WebSocket connection with an explanation.

units.description: When an app built with FastAPI needs to send something back to a client, it packages the reply in a specific shape. This unit provides the ready-made shapes: a page of HTML, plain text, JSON, a file download, a redirect instruction, a response that trickles data out over time, and a special live-update format called Server-Sent Events that lets a server keep pushing small updates to a page as they happen, like a chat feed or a progress bar.

units.name: request-datastructures
units.role: Defines UploadFile (FastAPI's async-friendly wrapper for an uploaded file) and the Default/DefaultPlaceholder sentinel mechanism used to detect caller-overridden defaults.
units.description: This unit provides basic building blocks other parts of FastAPI use to describe data coming in and out of a request. The most visible piece is UploadFile, the object a developer's code receives when a user uploads a file through a web form; it lets that code read, write, seek, and close the uploaded file asynchronously. The file also contains a small internal mechanism (Default and DefaultPlaceholder) FastAPI uses to tell whether a setting was explicitly chosen by a developer or left at its built-in default.

units.name: asgi-integrations
units.role: Re-exports Starlette's and anyio's ready-made ASGI building blocks (static files, templates, test client, request/websocket types, middleware) under the fastapi namespace, plus a helper for running blocking code off the event loop.
units.description: This part of the code does not implement new behavior itself. It acts like labeled doorways that let people write 'from fastapi import ...' and get proven, ready-made pieces, for serving static files, rendering HTML templates, testing an app, describing web requests and websocket connections, and adding common safety/compression middleware, that are actually built and maintained by a companion library called Starlette. One file also contains a small original helper that safely runs old-style blocking code in a background thread so it doesn't freeze the rest of the web server.

units.name: cli
units.role: Provides the `fastapi` command-line entrypoint, delegating to the optional fastapi-cli package.
units.description: This is the small piece of code that lets someone type the fastapi command in their terminal. It doesn't do the real work itself; if a separate optional tool called fastapi-cli is installed, it hands control over to that tool. If that tool is not installed, it prints a message telling the user to install it and stops with an error.

units.name: internal-helpers
units.role: Small shared support code (type aliases, the framework's log channel, and standalone helper functions) used across FastAPI's internals with no domain logic of its own.
units.description: This unit is a toolbox of small, generic building blocks that many other parts of FastAPI rely on but that do not, by themselves, represent any feature a developer using FastAPI would recognize: shared type labels used for internal bookkeeping, the named logging channel FastAPI uses to report messages, and small utility functions such as checking whether an HTTP status code is allowed to carry a body, pulling parameter names out of a URL path, building an internal field description from a Python type, generating a default unique name for a route, and merging two nested dictionaries.

violations_observed.note: openapi/utils.py imports underscore-prefixed 'private' helpers (_get_cache_key, _get_oauth_scopes, _get_security_scheme, _is_security_scheme, _get_flat_fields_from_params) directly from fastapi/dependencies/models.py and fastapi/dependencies/utils.py. They are listed here as dependency-injection entrypoints because they are genuinely called from outside the unit, but their underscore naming signals they were intended as private implementation details, not a public contract — the boundary between these two units is leakier than the naming suggests.

pydantic-compat is classified as infra (should only be depended upon by domain units), but v2.py does a local `from fastapi import params` inside is_scalar_field and checks `isinstance(..., params.Body)`. This is an infra unit reaching back into a domain unit's internals, the reverse of the intended layering, and it also creates a soft circular dependency since param-declarations itself imports Undefined from pydantic-compat.

api_key.py and open_id_connect_url.py raise starlette.exceptions.HTTPException directly instead of fastapi.exceptions.HTTPException, while http.py and oauth2.py use the fastapi subclass from the errors unit. Minor internal inconsistency, not a hard boundary violation, but means part of this unit bypasses the errors unit's own HTTPException entrypoint.
